facts.text: G.I. Joe was originally launched by Hasbro in 1964 as a 12-inch military action figure
Hasbro relaunched G.I. Joe in 1982 as a 3.75-inch 'A Real American Hero' line
The 1982 G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero toy line was supported by a Marvel Comics series written by Larry Hama
G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero became one of the best-selling toy lines of the 1980s
The G.I. Joe animated TV series launched in 1983 as a five-part mini-series and ended every episode with a public safety PSA
Snake Eyes, the silent commando in the G.I. Joe toy line, became the line's most popular figure
The G.I. Joe Cobra Commander figure was the primary villain of the line
Hasbro's G.I. Joe vehicle line included the MOBAT tank
The G.I. Joe: The Movie (1987) was produced alongside The Transformers: The Movie but went straight to home video
G.I. Joe figures in the 1980s featured a unique swivel-arm battle grip mechanism
At its peak in the mid-1980s, G.I. Joe generated over $125 million annually in toy sales for Hasbro
G.I. Joe's Defiant Space Launch Complex was the largest playset in the line, requiring hours to assemble
The Transformers toy line was launched by Hasbro in 1984
The original Optimus Prime Transformer toy in 1984 was a cab-over semi-truck that transformed into a robot
The Transformers animated series premiered in 1984 on the same day as the toy line's launch
The Transformers: The Movie (1986) killed off Optimus Prime in its first act
The Constructicons — six Transformers combining into Devastator — introduced the concept of combining robots
Soundwave, the Decepticon cassette player Transformer, was one of the most popular figures in the original line
The Japanese Transformers market developed in parallel with the American line under Takara
By 1985, Transformers was generating over $100 million annually for Hasbro
Megatron's original Transformer toy became a Walther P38 handgun with working trigger and detachable barrel extensions
The Dinobots — Grimlock, Slag, Sludge, Snarl, and Swoop — were Transformers that converted into mechanical dinosaurs
Fortress Maximus (1987) was nearly two feet tall — the largest Transformer toy ever made — and retailed for $99.99
The GoBots line by Tonka, based on Japan's Machine Robo, was Transformers' main rival before being absorbed into the Transformers universe
He-Man and the Masters of the Universe was launched by Mattel in 1982 and became an instant phenomenon
The He-Man toy line was the first accompanied by a dedicated animated series created purely to market the toys, setting a decade's template
Castle Grayskull (1982) featured a jaw-bridge entrance, a throne room, a working elevator, and a trap door dungeon
Skeletor was designed with blue skin and a bare skull face — initially controversial for being too frightening for a children's toy
She-Ra: Princess of Power (1985) was launched as a He-Man spin-off specifically targeting girls with a female hero protagonist
The He-Man toy line generated over $400 million in sales in 1984 alone
Mattel produced a live-action Masters of the Universe film in 1987 starring Dolph Lundgren as He-Man
He-Man's gray plastic 'Power Sword' was one of the most iconic and recognized toy accessories of the 1980s
Kenner's Star Wars action figures, launched in 1978, became one of the best-selling toy lines in history
The original Kenner Star Wars figure line used a 3.75-inch scale
Kenner produced over 100 different Star Wars figures between 1977 and 1985
The Kenner Millennium Falcon, released in 1979, was the largest Star Wars toy and a prized centerpiece of collections
Star Wars toy sales generated over $100 million for Kenner in 1978 alone
The Boba Fett action figure was originally announced with a spring-loaded rocket-firing backpack
The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles toy line launched by Playmates Toys in 1988 was considered a risky bet
The original Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles figures were produced in four distinct colors
Playmates Toys released over 400 different Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles figures throughout the line's run
The TMNT Party Wagon was the main vehicle playset in the toy line, mirroring the van from the animated series
Demand for TMNT toys in 1989 and 1990 was so intense that stores imposed purchase limits and parents lined up
Barbie was created by Ruth Handler and launched by Mattel at the 1959 American International Toy Fair
Barbie's full name is Barbara Millicent Roberts and she has held over 200 careers since her 1959 debut
The Barbie Dream House, first released in 1962, became one of the best-selling playsets in toy history
Ken, Barbie's boyfriend, was introduced by Mattel in 1961 and named after Ruth Handler's son Kenneth
By the 1980s, Barbie was generating over $500 million annually for Mattel
Totally Hair Barbie, launched in 1992, became the best-selling Barbie of all time with hair that extended to her feet
Barbie's proportions have been noted by researchers — if human-scale, she would be anatomically impossible to stand upright
Cabbage Patch Kids were originally hand-stitched 'Little People' sold at Georgia craft fairs before Coleco licensed the concept
The 1983 Cabbage Patch Kids Christmas rush became one of the most chaotic toy shortages in retail history
Each Cabbage Patch Kid came with a unique name printed on its birth certificate and an 'adoption paper'
Cabbage Patch Kids generated $600 million in sales in their first year of mass production in 1983
Hot Wheels were created by Mattel engineer Jack Ryan and designer Harry Bentley Bradley and launched in 1968
Hot Wheels' first track set, the Super Charger with orange track, used a battery-powered launcher to accelerate cars to scale speeds of 200 mph
Hot Wheels Redline cars (1968–1977) with their red-striped tires are among the most valuable die-cast collectibles
Mattel has produced over six billion Hot Wheels cars since 1968, making it the best-selling toy vehicle in history
Hot Wheels introduced the 'Sto & Go' playset series in the 1980s — compact folding playsets storing vehicles inside when closed
My Little Pony was created by designer Bonnie Zacherle at Hasbro and launched in 1982
Original 1980s My Little Pony figures are called 'G1' by collectors, featuring rooted brushable mane and tail hair
My Little Pony generated over $50 million in its first year and became one of Hasbro's most important and enduring toy franchises
Hasbro produced hundreds of My Little Pony variants in the 1980s including sea ponies
LEGO was founded in 1932 by Danish carpenter Ole Kirk Christiansen
LEGO bricks are manufactured to a tolerance of 0.002mm
LEGO Technic (1977) introduced gears, axles, and motors, allowing builders to create functional mechanical models
The LEGO Space theme, launched in 1978, was one of the most popular LEGO lines of the 1980s
LEGO Castle, launched in 1978, introduced minifigures
The LEGO Group nearly went bankrupt in 2003 after expanding too aggressively into electronics
It is estimated that there are approximately 80 LEGO bricks for every person on Earth
The Rubik's Cube was invented by Hungarian architect and professor Ernő Rubik in 1974

Rubik's Cube competitions, called speedcubing, began in 1981
The Rubik's Cube craze of 1980–1983 spawned an entire industry of solution books

The Speak & Spell gained pop culture immortality when it appeared in E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982)

Simon was inspired by Atari's arcade game Touch Me (1974)
Mattel Electronics released a line of handheld electronic sports games in the late 1970s
Teddy Ruxpin, launched by Worlds of Wonder in 1985, was the best-selling toy in America in both 1985 and 1986

Worlds of Wonder, Teddy Ruxpin's manufacturer, declared bankruptcy in 1987 after overexpanding, leaving production in limbo
The Super Soaker was invented by NASA engineer Lonnie Johnson in 1982 while he was working on a heat pump system
The Super Soaker 50 (1990) became the best-selling toy in America in 1991 and 1992, generating over $200 million in revenue
Super Soaker inventor Lonnie Johnson, an aerospace engineer, licensed the design to Larami and used royalties to fund energy research

Kenner acquired the Nerf brand in 1991 and launched the Nerf Blaster line starting with the Sharpshooter

By the mid-1990s, Nerf was generating over $100 million annually for Kenner

Mighty Morphin Power Rangers toys, launched in 1993, became one of the decade's best-selling action figure lines

Mighty Morphin Power Rangers generated over $1 billion in toy sales in its first two years

At the peak of the Pog craze in 1994, over 10 billion Pog caps were in circulation
Tamagotchi was created by Aki Maita at Bandai and launched in Japan in November 1996
Tamagotchi launched in the United States in May 1997 and sold over 40 million units globally in its first year
Bandai produced over 80 million Tamagotchis by the end of the 1990s
When a Tamagotchi's creature died, the device displayed a tombstone and had to be reset to start over
Micro Machines were created by Galoob in 1986 as miniature die-cast vehicles smaller than a matchbox car
Micro Machines became famous through their rapid-fire TV commercials voiced by John Moschitta Jr

The M.A.S.K. animated series, produced to support the toy line, ran for 75 episodes in 1985 and 1986
Voltron: Defender of the Universe was adapted from two separate Japanese anime series by World Events Productions
The Voltron die-cast and plastic toy produced by Matchbox in 1984 was one of the most sought-after holiday toys
ThunderCats the animated series premiered in 1985 and was developed specifically with a toy line in mind
The ThunderCats Sword of Omens toy was one of the most popular accessories in the line
Rock 'Em Sock 'Em Robots was invented by Marvin Glass and Associates and launched by Marx Toys in 1964
Rock 'Em Sock 'Em Robots was acquired by Mattel in the 1990s and remained a steady seller through the decade
Stretch Armstrong was created by developer J.C. Kuipers and launched by Kenner in 1976
Many children eventually cut open their Stretch Armstrong out of curiosity
Lite-Brite was invented by Marvin Glass and launched by Hasbro in 1967
Lite-Brite remained one of Hasbro's consistent sellers throughout the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s

Fisher-Price acquired View-Master in 1966 and by the 1980s released character reels for every major cartoon, movie, and toy franchise

Etch A Sketch's drawing system uses two knobs controlling horizontal and vertical movement of a stylus displacing aluminum powder

Over 3 billion cans of Play-Doh have been sold since 1956
Lincoln Logs were invented by John Lloyd Wright, son of architect Frank Lloyd Wright, in 1916
Lincoln Logs are one of the longest-produced toys in American history, remaining in production since 1916
The Erector Set was invented by A.C. Gilbert and launched in 1913 as one of the first construction toy systems
A.C. Gilbert saved toy chemistry sets and construction toys from a wartime ban in 1918 by convincing Congress

John Spinello invented Operation and sold the patent for $500 as a student, receiving nothing from its long success

Hungry Hungry Hippos is one of the loudest toys ever produced

Connect Four is a 'solved game' — meaning mathematically perfect play has been fully analyzed

Jenga was created by British game designer Leslie Scott
Jenga's 54 wooden blocks are precision-manufactured to be identical in size
Slap bracelets were invented by Wisconsin teacher Stuart Anders in 1983 and became one of the defining accessories
Slap bracelets sold over 10 million units in the United States in 1990 before the school ban wave peaked
Rainbow Brite was created by Hallmark and launched as a toy line by Mattel in 1983
The Rainbow Brite animated film released in 1985 was produced by DIC Entertainment and performed modestly
Strawberry Shortcake was created by Muriel Fahrion for American Greetings in 1977 and adapted into a toy line
The Strawberry Shortcake toy line pioneered the 'scented doll' category and proved so successful that competitors

Furby has been revised and relaunched multiple times since its 1998 debut
The Big Wheel was designed by Louis Marx and Company and launched in 1969

Weebles were introduced by Hasbro's Playskool in 1971 with the tagline 'Weebles wobble but they don't fall down.'
Skip-It was created by Tiger Electronics and launched in 1988
Tiger Electronics promoted Skip-It with an earworm commercial jingle
The yo-yo is one of the oldest toys in human history
The Yomega Brain (1984) featured an auto-return clutch, making it far easier to use than a traditional yo-yo

The Easy-Bake Oven was invented by Ronald Saarms and launched by Kenner in 1963
Kenner's Spirograph (1965) used interlocking plastic gears and a pen to create mathematical curve patterns on paper
The Atari 2600 was not just a gaming console but a cultural phenomenon that defined childhood in the early 1980s
The NES, released in North America in 1985, revived a crashed video game market and defined home gaming for a generation
Duncan Yo-Yos sold over 45 million units in 1962 alone

Kenner's Star Wars AT-AT Walker (1981) stood over 16 inches tall with opening hatches and removable figures

The California Raisins, created as ad characters in 1987, became an unexpected pop culture phenomenon spawning toys and TV specials
Pound Puppies were launched by Tonka in 1984 as stuffed dogs in cardboard 'pound' boxes with adoption certificates
Viewtron attempted to create an interactive information terminal in 1983 but failed commercially before the web existed

The Robotix system, launched by Milton Bradley in 1984, let kids build motorized robots from interlocking components
Shogun Warriors were a line of Japanese giant robot toys imported by Mattel in 1977
Wacky Packages were created by Art Spiegelman (who later created Maus) for Topps in 1967 as parody stickers
The baseball card market transformed in the 1980s into a serious speculative investment with rookie cards selling for hundreds of dollars
The 1989 Ken Griffey Jr. Upper Deck rookie card became one of the most valuable and iconic baseball cards
K'Nex was invented by Joel Glickman in 1992 after he noticed the geometric potential in a plastic straw
Tinkertoys, invented by Charles Pajeau in 1913, were inspired by watching children play with pencils and spools
Mouse Trap (1963) was a board game built around assembling an elaborate Rube Goldberg-style trap to catch opponents
Battleship was launched by Milton Bradley in 1967 based on a pencil-and-paper naval game that had been popular
The Speak & Spell spawned two sequels — Speak & Math and Speak & Read — completing Texas Instruments' electronic learning toy trio
The Beast Wars Transformers (1996) introduced animal alternate modes and launched a new generation of the franchise
LEGO Mindstorms (1998), named after Seymour Papert's book, let builders program LEGO robots using a drag-and-drop visual interface
Silly Putty was accidentally discovered by James Wright in 1943 while researching silicone rubber substitutes
Magna Doodle (1974) used magnetic particles suspended in liquid to create drawings that erased instantly
The Fisher-Price record player (1971) played color-coded plastic discs and was one of the first children's music toys
Fisher-Price redesigned Little People in 1985 from small wooden cylinders to larger plastic figures to eliminate choking hazards
Kenner's Ghostbusters toy line, launched alongside the 1984 film, introduced the concept of slime as a play feature
The Slip 'N Slide was invented by Robert Carrier and launched by Wham-O in 1961

The Fisher-Price Activity Center (1972) featured knobs, dials, and mirrors to stimulate infant development
